blocks.title: Read in Daily Life
blocks.passage:
Subject: Parking permits for the spring semester

Dear staff and students,
Parking permits for the spring semester can be purchased online from December 10. The price is €90 for students and €140 for staff. Permits are valid only in the zone indicated on the permit, and vehicles parked in other zones will be fined €35. Electric vehicles are eligible for a 50% discount, upon presentation of the registration document at the Service Desk. Permits cannot be transferred to another vehicle, but you may register up to two vehicles under one name (only one can be used at a time).

items.q: How much does a student permit cost?
What must a driver of an electric vehicle do to receive the discount?
options: Show the registration document at the Service Desk

items.q: What can be inferred about registering two vehicles?
options: Only one may be used at a time
items.explain: «only one can be used at a time».

blocks.title: Read an Academic Passage
blocks.passage:
The domestication of wheat about ten thousand years ago is often described as a leap forward, but some archaeologists now question that view. Skeletons from early farming communities show more signs of malnutrition and disease than those of earlier hunter-gatherers, suggesting that the shift to agriculture may initially have lowered living standards.

Why, then, did farming spread? One explanation is that farming could support far more people per unit of land. Even if individuals were less healthy, populations grew, and larger groups could displace smaller foraging bands. Another explanation emphasizes storage: grain could be saved, enabling communities to survive bad seasons, though it also created inequality, since those who controlled the stores gained power.

items.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why farming spread even though it may have lowered individual health

items.q: What do early farmers' skeletons show?
options: More signs of malnutrition and disease

items.q: "displace" is closest in meaning to
Why does the author mention storage?
options: To give a second explanation for the spread of farming

items.q: What can be inferred about grain stores?
options: They could concentrate power in the hands of a few

segments.text: Let's examine how cities can reduce flooding. Traditionally, engineers relied on gray infrastructure: concrete drains, tunnels and pumps. These are effective but expensive, and they only move water elsewhere. A growing alternative is called green infrastructure, which uses natural features to absorb rainwater.

A good example is the 'rain garden', a shallow depression filled with plants that soak up runoff from roofs and roads. In Philadelphia, thousands of such gardens have reduced the amount of water entering sewers by about a third. They also lower temperatures and provide habitats.

Of course, green infrastructure isn't a miracle cure. During extreme storms, it can be overwhelmed, so most cities use a mix of both approaches. The key is to plan them together, so that each compensates for the other's weaknesses.

items.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Using natural features and traditional systems to reduce urban flooding

items.q: What is a limitation of gray infrastructure?
options: It is expensive and only moves water elsewhere

items.q: Why does the professor mention Philadelphia?
options: To provide evidence of green infrastructure working
items.explain: Evidencia: una tercera parte menos de agua.

blocks.title: Write an Email
blocks.prompt:
**Situation.** You are the organizer of a student conference. A guest speaker has just informed you that she cannot attend because of illness. The conference is in three days.

**Write an email to the conference participants.** In your email:
- Inform them about the change.
- Explain what will replace her session.
- Reassure them and tell them where to find updates.
blocks.model:
Dear participants,

I regret to inform you that our guest speaker, Dr. Hall, cannot attend the conference because of illness. We wish her a quick recovery.

Her keynote will be replaced by a panel discussion with three faculty members, who will address the same topic at the same time on Friday at 10:00 a.m.

All other sessions remain unchanged, and any further updates will be posted on the conference website and sent by email. Thank you for your understanding, and we look forward to seeing you on Friday.

Best regards,
The Organizing Committee

blocks.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
blocks.prompt:
**Professor Patel:** Many universities now offer degrees entirely online. Do you think an online degree is as valuable as a traditional one?

**Sofia:** Yes, if the courses are well designed. Online degrees give access to people who cannot move or who must work.

**James:** I disagree. Campus life, labs, and personal contact with professors can't be replaced by a screen.

**Write a response** (≥ 110 words) with your opinion, a concession and a counterargument.
blocks.model:
I believe an online degree can be as valuable as a traditional one in many fields, though not in all. Sofia is right that online programs widen access. For example, a colleague of mine completed a business degree online while working full-time, and she is now a manager.

Admittedly, James is correct that laboratory work and personal contact matter. Nevertheless, many programs now combine online lectures with short on-campus periods, which keeps the benefits of both.

Therefore, the value of a degree depends less on the format than on the quality of the program and the support it offers.

questions.q: What is the biggest difference between studying at university and studying at school?
questions.model: The biggest difference is independence. At university, nobody checks whether you do your homework, so you must organize your own time. For example, in my first semester I missed a deadline because I underestimated a project, and that taught me to plan ahead.

questions.q: Do you think young people today read less than previous generations? Why or why not?
questions.model: I think they read differently rather than less. Instead of books, they read articles, messages and social media. However, long, deep reading has declined, which is a concern. For example, my younger cousin reads constantly online but struggles with long texts.
